topic: Choreographer, VSYNC, SurfaceFlinger & jank analysis with Perfetto

questions.question: On a 120 Hz display, roughly how long does the app have to produce each frame?
options: About 16 ms
About 8 ms
About 4 ms
About 12 ms
questions.explanation: The budget is one refresh period: 1000 ms / 120 is about 8.3 ms. The familiar 16 ms figure only applies at 60 Hz, which is why code that was fine on older phones can jank on high refresh rate screens.

questions.question: `Choreographer.getInstance()` is tied to the calling thread's Looper, so frame callbacks posted through it run on that thread, usually the main thread.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Choreographer is a per-Looper instance, and its callbacks are delivered on that Looper's thread. In practice that is the main thread, which is why slow frame callbacks delay input and drawing.

questions.question: When a VSYNC signal arrives, in which order does Choreographer run its main callback types for that frame?
options: Animation, then traversal, then input
Input, then animation, then traversal (measure/layout/draw)
Input, then traversal, then animation
Traversal (measure/layout/draw), then input, then animation
questions.explanation: Choreographer processes input first so the frame reflects the latest touch, then animations update values, then the traversal measures, lays out and draws using those values. Running animations after drawing would show stale positions.

questions.question: What does triple buffering buy an app, and what does it cost?
options: It removes the need for VSYNC, at the cost of screen tearing
It lets the app start the next frame while one buffer is shown and one is queued, at the cost of latency and memory
It doubles the frame rate, at the cost of higher GPU temperature
It lets two threads draw the same frame, at the cost of thread contention
questions.explanation: With a third buffer the app is not blocked waiting for the display to release a buffer, so an occasional slow frame can be absorbed. The trade-off is that a queued buffer adds a frame of input-to-display latency and needs extra memory. It does not raise the refresh rate.

questions.question: What is SurfaceFlinger's job in the frame pipeline?
options: Compositing buffers from all visible surfaces into the final image for the display, using the hardware composer or the GPU
Running inside each app process to pace its Choreographer
Decoding images for apps before they are drawn
Running each app's measure and layout passes
questions.explanation: SurfaceFlinger is a system process that takes the latest buffers from the status bar, your app's window and other layers and composes them for each display refresh. It does not run app code; apps render their own buffers and queue them to it.

questions.question: A Perfetto trace shows a 30 ms `Choreographer#doFrame` slice, but your code inside it should take 5 ms. Which main thread states during that slice would explain the extra wall time? Select all that apply.
options: Running: executing on a CPU core
Sleeping: blocked on a lock or a binder reply
Runnable: the thread was ready but waiting for a CPU
Uninterruptible sleep: waiting on I/O such as a page fault or disk read
questions.explanation: Wall time beyond your CPU work is time the thread spent not running: waiting for a core, blocked on I/O, or waiting on a lock or IPC. Each points to a different fix, such as reducing background contention or moving I/O off the main thread. Running time is your code itself, which you said was short.

questions.question: JankStats reports per-frame timing and lets you attach UI state, such as 'scrolling feed', so you can see what the app was doing when a frame was janky.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: JankStats delivers frame data with a jank flag and the current state values you register through its metrics state holder. That attribution is what makes production jank data actionable, instead of just a global percentage.

questions.question: In Perfetto's frame timeline, your app's frame finished within its expected window, but the actual frame was still late and the jank type is attributed to SurfaceFlinger. What is the right conclusion?
options: Your `onDraw()` is too slow and should be optimized first
The delay came from composition on the system side, so optimizing your app's frame work will not fix this frame
The trace is wrong because the app always owns the frame deadline
The app missed VSYNC because it posted too many frame callbacks
questions.explanation: The frame timeline compares expected and actual timelines for both the app and SurfaceFlinger and labels who missed the deadline. If the app was on time and the jank is attributed to SurfaceFlinger, the cause is in composition or the system, so app-side optimization will not help that frame.

questions.question: Which of these can make a frame miss its deadline even though `Choreographer#doFrame` itself is short? Select all that apply.
options: The GPU is still busy with earlier work, so the RenderThread waits for a free buffer
Long RenderThread work in `DrawFrame`, such as syncing large display lists or uploading textures
A low-priority background thread doing work on an otherwise idle multi-core device
A long `Handler` message runs on the main thread just before VSYNC, so `doFrame` starts late
Calling `postFrameCallback` once from a click listener
questions.explanation: The deadline covers the whole pipeline: when `doFrame` starts, RenderThread work and GPU completion. A message hogging the main thread delays the frame start even if the frame itself is short. Background work on an idle device and a single frame callback do not affect the main pipeline.

questions.question: During scroll jank, Perfetto shows a 40 ms `binder transaction` slice on the main thread, nested under `onBindViewHolder`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The RenderThread is blocking the main thread to upload textures
A synchronous call to a system service, such as a PackageManager or ContentResolver lookup, is running in bind
Kotlin coroutines use binder to switch dispatchers
RecyclerView is sending each item to SurfaceFlinger separately
questions.explanation: A binder transaction is IPC to another process, and in bind code it usually means a synchronous system service or content provider call. The main thread waits for the reply, so the fix is to load that data ahead of time off the main thread or cache it. RenderThread and coroutine dispatching do not show up as binder calls.
